topic: How Do Satellites Stay In Space Without Falling?
angle: They are actually falling down constantly at 28,000 kilometers per hour, but they never hit the ground because the Earth curves away underneath them.
why: Explainer videos about orbital mechanics and gravity routinely pull tens of millions of views because they challenge basic intuition. This question is irresistible because everyone looks up at the sky and wonders how heavy metal objects defy gravity without running out of fuel.
keywords: why satellites don't fall to earth
how do things stay in orbit
facts: Satellites in low Earth orbit travel at approximately 28,000 kilometers per hour, or about 8 kilometers per second.
At this extreme speed, as the satellite is pulled downward by Earth's gravity, the curvature of the Earth drops away at the exact same rate.
This continuous falling motion combined with forward momentum is what defines an orbit; it is a state of perpetual free fall.
There is still gravity in space; at the altitude of the International Space Station, about 400 kilometers up, Earth's gravity is still about 90% as strong as it is on the ground.
The reason astronauts float is not because there is no gravity, but because they and their spacecraft are falling together at the same acceleration.
Air resistance in the upper atmosphere, known as atmospheric drag, constantly slows satellites down, requiring periodic thruster burns to maintain their altitude.
Without correction burns, low Earth orbit satellites would eventually slow down, spiral inward, and burn up in the denser layers of the atmosphere.
Isaac Newton first conceptualized this exact principle in 1687 with his famous 'Newton's cannonball' thought experiment.
If a cannonball were fired fast enough from a high mountain, it would never hit the ground and would circle the entire planet.
Geostationary satellites orbit much higher, at about 35,786 kilometers above the equator, matching the exact rotational speed of the Earth.
At geostationary altitude, one full orbit takes 24 hours, making the satellite appear to hover stationary over a single point on the ground.
The energy required to reach orbit is almost entirely spent on gaining horizontal velocity rather than vertical height.
Modern satellite constellations like SpaceX's Starlink use automated ion propulsion systems to counteract atmospheric drag and adjust their orbits autonomously.
Britannica explains the mechanism behind Earth maintaining its stable path around the sun.
The New York Times reported on space debris being discovered twice within a span of days, noting an increasing casualty danger.
A farmer in Minnesota unexpectedly discovered an eleven-foot object during harvest that probably dropped from orbit.
A NASA spacecraft is currently monitoring the seasonal changes in leaf colors globally.
Publications have raised questions regarding the process of rocket remnants descending from orbit back to the ground.
